Title: Distributed, high-performance blob storage on SQLite - Zerodha Tech Blog

URL Source: https://zerodha.tech/blog/high-performance-distributed-blob-storage/

Markdown Content:
**TLDR;** We built Blobasaur, a sharded, distributed, lightweight blob storage server on top of SQLite to solve our high-throughput blob read/write usecase. JSON blobs varying from a few KBs to MBs are now written and read thousands of times per second on commodity hardware while maintaining single-digit millisecond latency.

* * *

On [Kite](https://zerodha.com/products/kite), our trading platform with ~20 million customers, users are able to customize their investment and trading screens heavily. They save multi-chart layouts, financial indicator templates, vector drawings, and various kinds of arbitrary UI preferences. In addition, we offer a Terminal mode that allows users to design their own workspaces by dragging, dropping, and customizing widgets. Under the hood, our backend services store these user preferences and metadata as opaque blobs (mostly JSON) ranging from a few kilobytes to several megabytes.

Many years ago, we stored such blobs in CouchDB, which turned out to be ill-suited for the kind of throughput we were starting to see. We then moved to SSDB ([ssdb](https://github.com/ideawu/ssdb)), a C++ disk-backed store that speaks the Redis protocol. This made it very easy to integrate as well. SSDB solved our immediate performance problems and ran reliably in production for several years.

Over time, two problems forced us to look for a replacement:

1.   SSDB became unmaintained, which was an obvious operational risk. It is written in C++, which is not a part of our stack or expertise, so forking and maintaining was also not viable.
2.   Scaling and size limits. SSDB is not a distributed system and can only run on a single node. This imposes significant future scaling challenges, including at one point forcing us to cap blob sizes at 1 MB because latency degrades on larger payloads.

As we added features like the Terminal mode and onboarded more internal services, we needed a robust solution. Our criteria were:

*   A key-value blob store with a simple API.
*   Designed for multi-megabyte blob read/write ops and high throughput. We sustain loads of thousands to tens of thousands of requests per second reading and writing arbitrary blobs. These are unpredictable and bursty thanks to the volatility in stock markets.
*   Horizontally scalable, distributed.
*   Disk-space efficiency / compression.
*   Easily maintainable and highly economical.

So we investigated FOSS databases optimized for high-throughput blob storage and looked at the following:

*   **ScyllaDB:** We already run ScyllaDB for high-throughput workloads, but in our tests, it turned out to be suboptimal for large blobs. Significantly lower throughput and higher resource usage. We specifically want multi-megabyte blobs. Tombstones from frequent overwrites and TTL expiries require careful tuning in ScyllaDB.
*   **PostgreSQL:** We already have [considerable experience](https://zerodha.tech/blog/working-with-postgresql/) with Postgres in our stack and experimented with storing blobs as `BYTEA` columns, but it turned out to be severely suboptimal again for the use case in terms of performance and disk-space efficiency.
*   **YugabyteDB:** Has blob storage as one of the options, but is not primarily designed or optimized for it. Also, a large system with too many features.
*   **RocksDB:** Had the right primitives, but again, not architected for high throughput multi-MB blob writes.
*   **Ceph:** Severe operational complexity and resource requirements. We didn’t even get to trying it out.
*   **SeaweedFS:** This was the closest candidate. However, there were a few blockers. Our use case is overwrite-heavy (a user changing their workspace) over the same key, and SeaweedFS keeps appending before compaction, which can cause disk usage to grow uncontrollably. Blobs have their own IDs, which then have to be mapped against user keys in a separate DB, adding another layer. It doesn’t support TTL per blob. Also, reasonably complex setup with many parts.
*   **S3 and MinIO:** Object storage has high per-request latency for small blobs, high request costs under write-heavy workloads (writes are 50% of our traffic), and coarse lifecycle TTLs instead of exact key expiry. Not to mention, S3 would incur significant costs given thousands of ops per second and tens of millions of ops per day.
*   **Raw filesystem (one file per blob):** Putting blobs directly on disk meant implementing atomic writes and write batching, managing large numbers of files and directories, good old atomic read/write disk performance and inode headaches, and maintaining a separate metadata index for TTLs. Not to mention, orchestrating this over AWS storage volumes.

Around this time, we were toying with SQLite for another project and were marveling at its [_35% Faster Than The Filesystem_](https://www.sqlite.org/fasterthanfs.html) claim. We also happen to have a query cache system that creates [millions of tables](https://nadh.in/files/indiafoss-2024-dungbeetle.pdf) every day in a Postgres instance, which pushes the database to its limits quite successfully. Putting two and two together, we thought, why not build a system on top of SQLite to store millions of blobs and see what happens?

So we ended up building [Blobasaur](https://github.com/iamd3vil/blobasaur), an open source sharded blob server written in Rust that speaks the Redis protocol and uses SQLite as its storage engine. It is a single binary application that is high performance, and super simple to deploy and maintain. It is in production at Zerodha and it has successfully replaced SSDB.

## What we needed

We had several Go and Python services already talking to SSDB via the Redis protocol, with more waiting to onboard. We wanted the new solution to meet these requirements:

*   Redis protocol compatibility (if possible at all): Every existing client already used standard Redis libraries (`GET`, `SET`, `HGET`, `HSET`, `DEL`, `EXPIRE`). If we could get a system that could be a drop-in replacement, that would allow us to leave existing services untouched and reduce risk significantly.
*   Low latency across payload sizes: It needed to serve both 2 KB settings blobs and 5 MB chart layouts with single-digit millisecond latency.
*   Built-in compression: Almost all our payloads are repetitive JSON, which compresses well.
*   Simple CRUD with TTLs: We didn’t need complex data structures, server-side scripting, or secondary queries. We just needed key-value and hash CRUD with key expiry.
*   Multi-node partitioning: We needed to split data across multiple machines so a single node wasn’t a bottleneck.
*   Relaxed durability is acceptable: This store holds non-critical UI and workspace preferences, and not critical financial data. If a sudden power loss drops recent writes, a user might lose a recent chart layout tweak, which is annoying, but it never affects trading. This was a good performance trade-off for our use case.

## Why SQLite (and Rust)

We had a few options for the storage. The obvious one is the raw filesystem, with one file per blob. But with that, we’d need to invent everything ourselves:

*   Atomic writes and batching.
*   TTL cleanup, which needs secondary indexes or walking the directories.
*   Dealing with fd limits.
*   Managing metadata separately from the raw data.

SQLite pretty much gave us everything that the raw filesystem lacked. For small blobs, SQLite is up to 35% faster than raw filesystem I/O. While raw files start to beat SQLite above ~100 KiB, we compress blobs before writing them. And thankfully, 99% of our compressed values sit well below 100 KiB.

Using SQLite also meant inheriting a battle-tested storage engine with ACID transactions, crash recovery, and standard tooling. Any shard on disk can be inspected with the standard `sqlite3` CLI or queried with plain SQL for analytics, etc.

While most of our backend stack is written in Go, we wrote Blobasaur in Rust. Go’s standard SQLite driver requires CGo, which complicates static builds, pins OS threads during C calls under high concurrency, and adds garbage-collection pressure when allocating and compressing multi-megabyte buffers. With Rust (`sqlx`, `rusqlite`, and `tokio`), we call SQLite’s C API directly with predictable memory usage and ship a single static binary.

## Architecture

### Splitting data into shards

In WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode, a single SQLite database allows concurrent readers, but still permits only one writer at a time. Since writes make up roughly 50% of our production traffic, a single SQLite file per node would bottleneck quickly.

To get write concurrency on a single machine, Blobasaur splits data across multiple SQLite database files on disk, called shards:

*   Consistent hashing: Each key maps to one shard via multi-probe consistent hashing.
*   Per-shard writer with group commit: Each shard has a dedicated writer task fed by a bounded queue. Instead of committing one key at a time, the writer drains a batch of pending writes from the queue and executes them inside a single `BEGIN IMMEDIATE ... COMMIT` transaction. This amortizes transaction and WAL overhead across concurrent clients.
*   Concurrent readers: Reads go directly to a per-shard pool of read-only SQLite connections and can run concurrently with the writer.

### How much does sharding help?

We benchmarked 1 shard against 16 shards using a load generator opening 64 concurrent connections. Each request used a 64 KiB JSON blob payload (close to our production average), which zstd compresses roughly 9x.

All runs used 100,000 keys, synchronous writes, and `batch_size = 50`, with the data directory on `tmpfs` to isolate SQLite locking and CPU overhead from disk variance. Both setups received the same total resources: 1,600 MB of SQLite page cache and 64 total read connections.

| Workload | 1 shard | 16 shards |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `HSET` only | 7,740 ops/s, p99 10.7 ms | 25,324 ops/s, p99 8.3 ms |
| 50% `HSET`, 50% `HGET` | 14,227 ops/s, p99 10.5 ms | 29,538 ops/s, p99 8.5 ms |
| `HGET` only | 67,128 ops/s, p99 2.1 ms | 70,884 ops/s, p99 2.3 ms |

With 16 shards, write throughput increases 3.3x and median write latency drops from 8.2 ms to 2.1 ms. Read throughput stays nearly identical because SQLite WAL mode already serves concurrent readers without contention.

At 25,324 `HSET` operations per second, each carrying a 64 KiB payload, Blobasaur processes roughly **1.66 GB/s of uncompressed JSON** through zstd. Both the server and load generator ran on the same 16-core laptop, sharing its CPU resources.

### Schema

Our services use both plain keys (`SET`/`GET`) and Redis hashes (`HSET`/`HGET`) to group blobs by service or feature (for example, `HSET prefs userID <json>`).

Inside each shard, plain keys live in a `blobs` table:

```
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS blobs (
    key TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    data BLOB,
    created_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
    updated_at INTEGER NOT NULL,
    expires_at INTEGER,
    version INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);

CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_expires_at
    ON blobs(expires_at)
    WHERE expires_at IS NOT NULL;
```

`SET` writes to `blobs`. `HSET` writes to a table for its namespace, `blobs_<namespace>`, with the same columns. For example, `HSET prefs user42 ...` stores `user42` in `blobs_prefs`.

Expiry is stored in `expires_at` on the same row. Read queries filter out expired rows at read time (`expires_at IS NULL OR expires_at > ?`), while a background worker reaps expired rows asynchronously. Because the index on `expires_at` is a partial index (`WHERE expires_at IS NOT NULL`), rows without a TTL take up no space in the expiry index.

### Compression

Blobasaur supports zstd, lz4, gzip, and brotli compression before writing to SQLite. We run zstd in production.

articles.content:
Title: The 98% Slot Machine

URL Source: https://globalcommercegraph.com/writing/the-ninety-eight-percent-slot-machine

Published Time: 2026-11-11

Markdown Content:
There is a quiet tragedy that plays out every morning in the dashboard of Google Ads and Meta Business Suite.

A founder sits down with their coffee, opens their ad account, and looks at the numbers. Yesterday they spent $420. They booked one sales call and got one small order. After fulfillment costs, they made roughly $410.

A net loss of ten dollars.

A normal person walking away from a slot machine down ten dollars would recognize they lost. But the ad dashboard doesn't present it as a loss. It presents it as a near-miss. It serves up a carousel of green percentage metrics: impressions up 14%, click-through rate up 0.2%, cost-per-click down 4 cents.

The founder tells themselves the same lie that has kept Las Vegas casinos in business for seventy years: _“We’re dialed in. We’re just one sale away from break-even.”_

So they press the button again. They fund the account for another week. They tweak the headline, swap the creative, test a lookalike audience, and feed another five thousand dollars into the machine.

They don't realize they aren't running an acquisition channel. They are playing a digital slot machine calibrated by hyperscalers to pay out at exactly 98%.

### The Mathematics of the Near-Miss

A casino slot machine that pays out 50% doesn't make money. The gambler loses too fast, realizes the game is rigged, feels the sting of the loss, and stands up.

A casino slot machine that makes billions is calibrated to hover between 92% and 98%. It returns just enough small wins to keep dopamine dripping into the gambler's prefrontal cortex. You put in twenty dollars, it hands back eighteen dollars with loud bells and flashing lights, and you convince yourself that with a little more patience, the jackpot is three pulls away.

Ad auctions are engineered on the exact same psychological exploit.

If Google and Meta handed you a 100% predictable loss on day one, you would cancel your credit card and hire a sales rep. But if you spend $1,000 and get $900 back, you blame your landing page. You blame your copywriter. You blame your checkout flow.

You never blame the auction house.

### The Inherent Flaw of the Auction Model

The dirty secret of performance marketing is that the platform's business model requires your margins to drop to zero.

When an ad platform is young and inventory is cheap, early advertisers make absurd returns. In 2012, you could run Facebook ads for a dental practice or an e-commerce shop and print 5x returns all day. That wasn't because the ads were genius; it was because the auction was empty.

As more businesses enter the auction, bid prices rise. But they don't rise to a reasonable market rate. They rise to the absolute maximum point of economic tolerance: the exact dollar amount where the advertiser is breaking even on their gross margin.

The auction algorithm is an extraction machine designed to capture all economic surplus. The moment you find a keyword or audience that yields an extra 20% margin, competitors bid up that same inventory. Within six months, that 20% surplus margin is transferred entirely into the ad platform's quarterly revenue report.

The winners of the auction don't "win" profits. They win the privilege of working for free as unpaid fulfillment contractors for Google and Meta, turning raw revenue into ad spend.

### The Silent Exit

Most businesses don't crash with a bang. They just quietly run out of runway.

They spend six months or two years in "one sale away" mode. They burn through their seed capital, their line of credit, or their retained earnings. One morning, the credit card bounces on the ad account. The traffic drops to zero instantly. There is no residual equity, no organic momentum, and no customer relationship that belongs to the business.

The ad account goes dark. Google doesn't send a condolence note. The auction algorithm doesn't skip a beat. It simply reallocates those impressions to the next hopeful founder standing in line with a fresh $10,000 credit limit.

### What Lies Outside the Casino

The platform squeeze worked because it convinced an entire generation of entrepreneurs that the only way to reach a buyer is to rent their attention from a landlord.

We were told that if you don't buy Google keywords, you don't exist. If you don't run paid social ads, you have no pipeline.

Meanwhile, right underneath that screaming, overfished casino, billions of dollars in commercial trade change hands every single day between companies that have never spent a nickel on a Meta ad in their history.

A specialized 20-person packaging plant in Indiana doesn't gamble on Facebook lookalike audiences. An agricultural tax advisory firm doesn't bid on Google search terms. They operate through durable commercial relationships: trade guilds, supply chain dependencies, regional partner networks, and non-peer referral circles.

The internet you can buy through an ad auction is a crowded, hyper-expensive 30% slice where the house always wins.

The other 70% of the economy is out in the open air, trading quietly with people they actually know. The only way to reach them isn't to feed more money into the slot machine, but to step off the casino floor entirely.

### Pete Warden on Local AI, Open Models, Voice Interfaces, and the Future of Hardware.

**Subscribe:**[**Apple**](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/the-data-exchange-with-ben-lorica/id1487704458)**•**[**Spotify**](https://open.spotify.com/show/65oFWYoomwT8mLcdGkUGd0)**•**[**Overcast**](https://overcast.fm/itunes1487704458)**•**[**Pocket Casts**](https://pca.st/kv9n4vc0)**•**[**YouTube**](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLnTmH22EvTFTtWJRPTNzosDIDblnSg0PD)**•**[**AntennaPod**](https://antennapod.org/deeplink/subscribe/?url=feeds.buzzsprout.com/682433.rss)**•**[**Podcast Addict**](https://podcastaddict.com/podcast/2476584)**•**[**Amazon**](https://music.amazon.com/podcasts/18e76845-60a8-4263-9c41-a7bdfe9d14a9/the-data-exchange-with-ben-lorica)**•**[**RSS**](https://feeds.buzzsprout.com/682433.rss)**.**

[**Pete Warden**](https://petewarden.com/), co-creator of [**Moonshine Voice**](https://www.moonshine.ai/) and a longtime deep learning engineer, joins me to discuss why AI increasingly wants to run locally rather than in the cloud. We explore the rapid progress of open-weight models, what it takes to run AI on laptops and in browsers, and how low-latency speech models could make voice a more natural interface. We also discuss specialized versus end-to-end models, the economics of local AI, and emerging hardware approaches that could challenge today’s GPU-centric infrastructure. [This episode originally aired on [**Generative AI in the Real World**](https://learning.oreilly.com/playlists/42123a72-1108-40f1-91c0-adbfb9f4983b/), a podcast series I’m hosting for O’Reilly.]

### Transcript

Below is a**polished and edited transcript**.

**Ben Lorica.** All right. Today we have an old friend, Pete Warden of Useful Sensors, and their main website is actually at moonshine.ai. If you go to the website, you’ll see that they’re very much about voice on-device, and we will definitely talk to Pete about all things speech and all things edge computing. But I do want to take advantage of Pete being one of the OG deep learning engineers to get his sense of what’s going on these days. And with that, Pete, welcome back to the podcast.

**Pete Warden.** Thanks for having me, Ben.

**Ben Lorica.** All right. So I would say, Pete, I don’t know if this is a fair characterization, but one of the main thrusts of your work is the whole idea that local AI does not have to be compromised. In fact, it’s something that people should take more seriously. As I mentioned, we’ll definitely talk about your work on speech models on-device. But broadly speaking, Pete, for our audience that doesn’t really follow local models, where are we for someone who wants to run a model on a laptop, not a phone, just a laptop? What’s the state of ease of use? I guess one of the obstacles is that it’s always easier to use a cloud API, right? So where are we in terms of the tooling around local AI?

**Pete Warden.** Yeah. So at the moment, it’s like many open-source projects. Every year is going to be the year of the Linux desktop. I think there’s always going to be a bit of a lag in usability for the average user with this stuff, but I think there’s an even bigger lag in marketing because it’s very hard to make money off local models.

That means the big companies like Anthropic and OpenAI, and even the big tech companies generally, aren’t going to push that. If you give them a choice between a SaaS service that you can actually make money on and this other thing where you’re not even going to know that people are using it because they’re not contacting your service, every company is going to go for the one that has an easy subscription revenue model.

That means you have a massive amount of marketing around all of these tools that are basically a little text box on a website. And so it means that most people have never heard of these local models.

Now, if you use something like Ollama, which is probably the most well-known, I think people will be pleasantly surprised by how straightforward it is to use and by the quality of the models. I saw some news recently that Anthropic is actually a bit concerned because people are turning to more specialized models versus always going for the most sprawling, expensive model that’s available.

Local models are actually doing very well in the benchmarks. They continue to be only a few months behind the capabilities of the big commercial Anthropic and OpenAI models. But I also believe that local models have gotten to the point where they can do the things that people want to use them for.

What I’m really hoping is that it’s one of those situations, for those of us old enough to remember the dot-com boom, when people were paying thousands of dollars for SPARC servers or using Microsoft IIS and paying massive amounts of money because web servers were seen as such an arcane thing. Then, of course, Apache, Nginx, and all of these alternatives, once people actually had time to look around and the alternatives had a little bit of time to improve, just wiped the floor with the commercial alternatives.

I don’t know if we’re going to quite get there, but that’s the pattern I’m seeing.

**Ben Lorica.** Yeah, my sense is that open models, whatever your definition of open is, mainly open weights, I guess, will ultimately prevail. It just seems like that makes a lot more sense to me.

As you mentioned, in the early days of Linux versus Solaris, or even Postgres and MySQL versus Oracle, it was far from clear that these open-source projects would ever get to the point of us having to take them seriously. But ultimately, I think they’re such important parts of the stack that the open alternatives are what people will opt for.

Speaking of which, Pete, you mentioned Ollama, right? And obviously, there are other alternatives. Let’s say, for the sake of argument, that they are in fact easy to install and use. As far as the models are concerned, you have things like Gemma, I suppose, and other small models, right? What kind of hardware does someone need to have in order to run these models so that they don’t have to wait 20 minutes for each prompt?

**Pete Warden.** So a lot of it comes down to your model choice.

**Ben Lorica.** Yeah.

**Pete Warden.** You can get very capable models that are like 9 billion parameters these days. Especially if you look around at the Qwen family of models, they tend to be doing very well, though there are a bunch of other alternatives.

**Ben Lorica.** But translate that, Pete. To someone with a normal laptop, is 9 billion big or small?

**Pete Warden.** So the key thing is whether you can fit that into your graphics card’s memory. With weight quantization, 9 billion, if it was eight bits, is like nine gigabytes. A lot of decent midrange laptops that are shipping now have more than that.

But using Q4, and there are all sorts of schemes, you can actually get that down into a four-gigabyte graphics card, and that’s widely available. There are a lot of even older laptops that have that amount of GPU memory, VRAM, in them.

So really, the hardware barriers are a lot lower than people think. And the other piece of good news is that all of the hardware manufacturers are looking at this. They’re slightly hobbled by the DRAM craziness, the price increases. But if you look at the new M5 Studio from Apple, they have a configuration that’s 256 gigabytes of system memory.

Apple does a great job of actually making that available to the accelerators that they build into all of their Macs now, too. And with that, you’re looking at something like a model with hundreds of billions of parameters that you can actually run at a decent speed.

Once you get up into those numbers, you’re really looking at something where it can be hard to tell if you’re using Claude or if you’re using an open-weights model at that point. They have different characteristics, but one isn’t clearly worse than the other.

**Ben Lorica.** So as I mentioned, we’ll definitely dive deep into voice and speech in a second here. But sticking with this notion of local models, obviously privacy and IP security are arguments for it.

Do you think, if we look ahead, let’s say 12 to 24 months, these local models are going to be capable enough that people doing knowledge work in an enterprise might even consider them here and there?

For example, someone who travels a lot is on an airplane, not connected to the internet, and needs to keep writing a document or generating images or even coding, vibe coding, on a laptop. Do you think we’ll get to the point where, with these local models, you essentially feel like you’re not compromising when you’re doing your knowledge work?

**Pete Warden.** I think you can actually get to that point right now, and I know that’s a fairly bold statement.

**Ben Lorica.** But when you say you, does that mean Pete Warden, who’s going to compile all of these? We want normal people. We want civilians, Pete.

**Ben Lorica.** Model quality.

**Pete Warden.** Yeah, a question of model quality. There are still things around the edges where you might prefer some of the commercial online models, but it’s not clear-cut.
